text:
Escalating to human for design clarification before claiming. Three substantive design questions surfaced while planning the implementation:

## Q1: `issuer` parameter shape

The wrapper signature in the bead description is:

```rust
pub fn verify_ocsp_responder<P, R>(
    chain: &[Certificate],
    anchors: &[TrustAnchor],
    issuer: &Certificate,
    profile: &P, now_unix: u64, revocation: &R,
) -> ...
```

The `issuer` is "the CA whose certs the responder asserts status on" (RFC 6960 §4.2.2.2). The delegation check requires both:

- `responder.issuer_dn == issuer.subject_dn` (DN equality, RFC 4518).
- `responder.signature` verifies under `issuer.spki`.

But verify_chain ALREADY enforces (b) when issuer is in the chain (the responder's signature is verified during path validation against chain[1].spki). And if chain[1] is the issuer arg, the wrapper just needs to assert chain[1] == issuer (DN equality).

**Options:**

- (A) `issuer: &Certificate` — caller passes a full cert; wrapper checks `chain[1].subject == issuer.subject` (DN). Redundant for the signature half (verify_chain did it). Most explicit at the call site.
- (B) `issuer: &TrustAnchor` — caller wraps the CA as a TrustAnchor; wrapper checks `chain[1].subject == anchor.subject`. Awkward — TrustAnchor is semantically a *root*, not an intermediate.
- (C) `issuer_subject: &Name` — caller passes only the DN. Lightweight. Loses the SPKI cross-check (already done by verify_chain).
- (D) Drop the `issuer` arg entirely. Caller is responsible for arranging chain so chain[1] is the relevant issuer. Wrapper just runs verify_chain + EKU + nocheck.

(D) is tempting but loses the explicit "responder must be delegated by THIS issuer" assertion at the API. Recommend (A) for API clarity; the DN-equality check is cheap.

## Q2: Self-signed (CA-direct) OCSP signing

RFC 6960 §4.2.2.2 explicitly allows the CA to sign OCSP responses directly (no delegation). In that case the "responder cert" IS the issuer cert. Wrapper behavior:

- (A) Reject (force delegation). Cleaner type discipline; some real-world deployments don't delegate.
- (B) Accept if chain is single-cert and equals issuer. Adds branching in the wrapper.
- (C) Caller distinguishes by passing chain=[issuer] vs chain=[responder, issuer]. Wrapper logic handles both.

Recommend (C) — natural shape, no API surface explosion.

## Q3: id-pkix-ocsp-nocheck (RFC 6960 §4.2.2.2.1)

When the responder cert carries this extension (OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.48.1.5), the verifier MUST skip revocation checking of the responder cert (otherwise infinite OCSP loop).

The wrapper takes a `revocation: &R` arg that gets passed to verify_chain. verify_chain calls `revocation.check_revocation(cert, issuer)` for every cert. To honor nocheck on chain[0] specifically, the wrapper must somehow short-circuit just that call.

**Options:**

- (A) Pre-check for nocheck on chain[0]; if present, wrap the caller's `revocation` in a shim that returns Ok(()) for chain[0] and delegates everything else. Cleanest, no verify_chain change needed.
- (B) Add a nocheck-aware revocation method to RevocationChecker trait (touches pkix-revocation API).
- (C) Skip the nocheck rule entirely in v0.x. Document the gap. Callers who care can pre-strip the responder cert from the revocation oracle's view.

Recommend (A). Shim approach keeps everything local to verify_ocsp_responder.

## My overall recommendation

(Q1=A, Q2=C, Q3=A). All three are non-breaking; if Mark prefers other answers I can pivot quickly. The signature ends up looking like:

```rust
pub fn verify_ocsp_responder<P, R>(
    chain: &[Certificate],   // [responder, issuer] OR [issuer] (self-signed case)
    anchors: &[TrustAnchor],
    issuer: &Certificate,
    profile: &P,
    now_unix: u64,
    revocation: &R,
) -> Result<ValidatedPath, Error>
```

with wrapper body:

1. Build a `NoCheckRespRevocation` shim around `revocation` that returns Ok(()) for chain[0] iff chain[0] carries id-pkix-ocsp-nocheck.
2. `verify_chain(chain, anchors, &profile.policy(now), &DefaultVerifier, &shim)`.
3. Delegation check: if chain.len() > 1, assert chain[1].subject == issuer.subject; otherwise assert chain[0] is issuer itself.
4. Return Ok(validated).

Filing as human-labeled — answers turn into a fast implementation session afterwards.
